case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the First Amendment permits a state attorney general to enforce or investigate alleged “deceptive” speech by a nonprofit advocacy organization through compelled disclosures (e.g., subpoenas/civil investigative demands), and what standard governs pre-enforcement First Amendment challenges to that enforcement activity.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. I (free speech and associative rights), as applied through 42 U.S.C. § 1983 / Ex parte Young-style prospective relief; and New Jersey’s consumer-protection enforcement authority (referenced in the record through use of the New Jersey Consumer Fraud Act investigative tools).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: First Choice Women’s Resource Centers, Inc. argues that New Jersey’s investigative/enforcement tactics—particularly compelled production of internal information and other burdens associated with consumer-fraud investigation—function as an unconstitutional regime of compelled disclosure and chilled speech targeted at a viewpoint-driven speaker (a pro-life pregnancy center). It contends that even without a completed enforcement action, the investigation itself imposes First Amendment injury (speech chill and associational harms), is not narrowly tailored, and should be subject to heightened scrutiny and meaningful pre-enforcement judicial review rather than deference typical of ordinary subpoena enforcement. Petitioner and its amici further argue that courts should not dismiss such claims using mislabeled threshold doctrines (e.g., “prudential standing” or other justiciability-like filters), invoking Lexmark’s clarification that ‘prudential standing’ labels can obscure the real question—whether the plaintiff has a cause of action and whether the asserted interests fall within the protected zone (here, core First Amendment interests).
case_analysis.respondent_position: Attorney General Platkin maintains that New Jersey is conducting a lawful consumer-protection investigation into potentially deceptive advertising or practices, using standard investigative tools, and that such investigation does not itself violate the First Amendment absent proof of improper targeting, lack of legitimate purpose, or undue burden under established subpoena/CID standards. Respondent’s position (as reflected in the procedural posture and related state-court discussion) also emphasizes comity and orderly administration: challenges to investigative demands should proceed through ordinary mechanisms (e.g., motions to quash in state court), and parallel proceedings may warrant stays or abstention-like restraint where a state enforcement/investigation process is ongoing and provides an adequate forum to raise constitutional objections.
key_precedents: Lexmark Int’l, Inc. v. Static Control Components, Inc., 572 U.S. 118 (2014)
Platkin v. Smith & Wesson Sales, 474 N.J. Super. 476 (App. Div. 2023)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s administrability point is the strongest counter: ordinary subpoena-enforcement procedures often can sort relevance, burden, and confidentiality without turning every CID into a constitutional case. But our NAACP/AFP line treats compelled disclosure of supporter-identifying and internal advocacy information as a present associational injury capable of chilling participation, and the availability of later enforcement review does not erase the coercive choice at the moment of demand. As Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson warn, we should not constitutionalize routine investigations; the way to meet that concern is a narrow holding that allows pre-enforcement review only for associationally sensitive categories and remands for request-by-request application of exacting scrutiny (substantial relation to a sufficiently important interest, with tailoring calibrated to the actual burden). Justice Kagan’s emphasis that generalized investigative convenience cannot carry the State’s burden where narrower avenues remain supports that limited disposition.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Jackson raise the strongest point: we should not constitutionalize routine consumer-fraud investigations or convert every relevance dispute into a First Amendment claim. But that framing assumes the compelled demand is merely “incidental,” when (as the Chief Justice and Justice Alito explain) compulsory process that reaches supporter-identifying and internal advocacy materials imposes an immediate associational burden—comply and chill association, or resist and face sanctions—triggering heightened scrutiny at the moment of demand under our NAACP/AFP line. Ordinary motion-to-quash procedures do not answer the threshold constitutional question whether these speech-implicating categories are necessary; the State must justify them with genuine narrow tailoring (and, in my view, strict scrutiny for content-based demands). A narrow disposition allowing pre-enforcement review for those sensitive categories, with category-by-category tailoring on remand, addresses administrability without immunizing dragnet demands from First Amendment limits.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Jackson make the strongest point on administrability: routine CIDs are ordinarily policed through motions to quash and enforcement proceedings, and we should not constitutionalize every relevance or burden dispute by labeling it “chill.” But that framing overlooks that, under NAACP and Americans for Prosperity—as the Chief Justice stresses—the First Amendment injury can occur at the moment the State compels production of supporter-identifying and internal advocacy materials, because the coercive choice (comply or face sanctions) is immediate and predictably chilling. Relegating review to a later enforcement/contempt posture invites the very leverage problem we have condemned in Bantam Books: the State can impose the chill first and litigate later, even without an “informal” censorship scheme. I would therefore favor a narrow disposition recognizing pre-enforcement review where compulsory process targets associationally sensitive advocacy materials and remanding for category-by-category exacting-scrutiny tailoring, rather than enjoining investigative authority in gross.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justice Kagan rightly stress that compelled disclosure of supporter-identifying or internal advocacy materials can itself impose an immediate NAACP/AFP-type associational burden, and in that subset of cases pre-enforcement review may be appropriate. But Justice Kavanaugh and Justice Jackson have the better framework-matching point on this pleadings record: what is alleged looks primarily like routine consumer-fraud compulsory process, cabined by motion-to-quash/enforcement proceedings and confidentiality safeguards, rather than a Bantam Books-style coercive campaign to suppress disfavored advocacy. Without a concrete showing that the CID actually compels donor/member rosters or comparably sensitive associational lists (or otherwise communicates a threat aimed at suppressing protected expression), treating issuance alone as a completed First Amendment violation risks constitutionalizing ordinary investigations and invites unadministrable line-drawing. The proper course is to require category-by-category tailoring objections to be litigated in the enforcement posture on a developed record, while leaving open exacting scrutiny if truly associationally sensitive disclosures are compelled.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s administrability point is the strongest on the other side: in the mine-run CID, First Amendment objections can—and often should—be handled through the ordinary motion-to-quash/enforcement process. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, that assumes the speech/association burden is merely incidental, whereas these pleadings plausibly describe compelled production of supporter-identifying and internal advocacy materials—burdens our NAACP/AFP line treats as present and chilling at the moment of demand, not “beside the point” until contempt. The availability of later narrowing or confidentiality does not answer why the State needs these associationally sensitive categories in the first place; generalized investigative convenience is not a substantial-relation, proportionately tailored justification under exacting scrutiny. The narrow way through, consistent with Justice Roberts’s proposal, is to allow pre-enforcement review only for those associationally sensitive categories and remand for category-by-category exacting-scrutiny tailoring, rather than constitutionalizing every subpoena.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is administrability: courts should not constitutionalize every CID based on generalized allegations of chill, especially where motion-to-quash practice can test relevance and burden. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, our NAACP/AFP line treats compelled disclosure of supporter-identifying and internal advocacy materials as a present First Amendment injury because the target immediately faces a coercive choice—speak as the State demands or risk sanctions—and that is not cured by the prospect of later enforcement litigation. The limiting principle is workable and familiar: exacting scrutiny is triggered only when compulsory process reaches associationally sensitive rosters or internal strategy of an ideological speaker, and the State must show a substantial relation and tailoring beyond investigative convenience. As Justice Barrett notes, § 1983 and Ex parte Young exist to permit timely judicial review before the State extracts constitutionally protected information, so pre-enforcement review here fits settled remedial pathways without turning every subpoena dispute into a First Amendment case.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The Chief Justice and Justices Kagan, Gorsuch, and Barrett press the strongest point: NAACP and Americans for Prosperity recognize that compelled disclosure of supporter-identifying or internal advocacy material can itself be a present First Amendment injury, and the coercive choice exists upon service of compulsory process. But that principle must be tightly matched to what is actually compelled here; on this pleadings record, as Justice Jackson emphasizes, we lack a concrete showing that the CID in fact demands donor/member rosters or comparably sensitive associational lists (as opposed to transaction-specific evidence relevant to alleged deception), and converting generalized “chill” allegations into a categorical pre-enforcement First Amendment bypass would constitutionalize routine investigations and require unadministrable line-drawing. I would keep the ordinary motion-to-quash/subpoena-enforcement framework as the vehicle for category-by-category narrowing, while leaving open that, on a developed record showing true NAACP/AFP-type compelled disclosure, exacting scrutiny could apply at the enforcement stage. Justice Roberts’s proposed “narrow holding” still risks blurring that administrable boundary because it invites immediate constitutional litigation whenever an ideological speaker asserts sensitivity, without the concrete predicate NAACP/AFP require.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is administrability: if any subpoena recipient can plead “chill,” we risk constitutionalizing routine relevance and burden disputes better handled in motion-to-quash practice. But our compelled-disclosure cases—NAACP and Americans for Prosperity—treat demands for supporter-identifying and internal advocacy materials as a present First Amendment injury because the coercive choice is immediate, and § 1983/Ex parte Young presuppose pre-enforcement review when state process itself creates that pressure (as Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize). The way to accommodate Kavanaugh’s concern is not to require contempt, but to adopt a tight trigger: pre-enforcement review only for demands that, on their face or plausibly as pleaded, seek associational rosters or internal advocacy strategy, with exacting-scrutiny tailoring assessed category-by-category on remand. That rule preserves ordinary subpoena administration while preventing compulsory process from extracting constitutionally sensitive associational information before a court can test necessity and fit.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s point that compelled disclosure of supporter-identifying or internal advocacy information can itself be a present associational injury subject to exacting scrutiny, and thus may be reviewable without waiting for sanctions. But that observation does not answer the antecedent, framework-matching question: what First Amendment theory is properly in play on this pleadings record—an NAACP-style compelled-membership-list burden, a Bantam Books–type informal censorship campaign, or instead routine compulsory process subject to narrowing and confidentiality protections in an enforcement/quash proceeding. As Justice Kavanaugh emphasizes, without a concrete showing that the CID actually compels donor/member rosters or comparably sensitive associational lists (as opposed to transaction-specific evidence relevant to alleged deception), generalized “chill” allegations risk converting ordinary investigations into categorical pre-enforcement First Amendment bars. I would therefore leave room for targeted associational-privacy objections under exacting scrutiny on a developed record, but reject broad pre-enforcement invalidation here.

John Roberts.reasoning: A state attorney general’s compelled production of a nonprofit advocacy organization’s sensitive internal and supporter information—invoked here to police allegedly “deceptive” advocacy about a contested public issue—triggers First Amendment associational protections under NAACP v. Alabama and is reviewed under exacting scrutiny. The record, as described, indicates a serious “actual burden” on association (deterrence and chill from forced disclosure of donor/supporter information in a politically charged context), while the State’s justification sounds largely in generalized investigative efficiency (seeking a “representative sample”) rather than a concrete, narrowly focused need tied to a particularized fraud claim. Under exacting scrutiny, New Jersey must show a substantial relation between the specific disclosures demanded and a sufficiently important interest, with tailoring that matches the burden’s seriousness; on these facts, a dragnet-style demand for donor lists and internal materials is not adequately justified or tailored when less intrusive investigative avenues remain available. Pre-enforcement review is appropriate because the compelled-disclosure injury is the investigation’s coercive demand itself, which can chill association before any final enforcement action.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: New Jersey’s use of consumer-fraud investigative tools to demand a nonprofit advocacy organization’s internal materials and donor-identifying information imposes a direct First Amendment burden on speech and associational anonymity, triggering at least “exacting scrutiny” with narrow tailoring—and, in my view, strict scrutiny like other direct First Amendment burdens. On this record, the State’s asserted interest in policing “deception” does not justify compelled disclosure absent a concrete, narrowly tailored showing that the specific information sought is necessary and that less speech-restrictive means (including subpoenas limited to non-associational, non-donor information) would be inadequate. The investigation itself can inflict a cognizable, objective chill and associational injury before any contempt order where the demanded disclosures predictably deter donors and constrain advocacy, so the First Amendment claim should not be dismissed on threshold, abstention-like, or “prudential standing” rationales. Because the State has not shown narrow tailoring to a compelling (or sufficiently important) interest as applied to these compelled disclosures, the First Amendment bars this enforcement approach on the present facts.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The challenged conduct is not “government speech” but the State’s use of compulsory process (a subpoena/CID) to obtain internal information from a viewpoint-driven advocacy organization, and the First Amendment forbids the government from using investigative tools as an indirect means to burden or suppress disfavored speech. On this record and procedural posture, a rule that forces the target to wait until a subpoena is enforced in full before any federal judicial review would invite precisely the kind of coercive, chilling pressure Bantam Books and Vullo condemn, especially where the compelled disclosures implicate associational and internal-strategy information protected by cases like Americans for Prosperity. Pre-enforcement relief is appropriate when the investigative demand itself imposes a present First Amendment injury (chill and compelled disclosure) and the State has not shown a sufficiently tailored need for the breadth of what it seeks. At minimum, the federal courts should not dismiss on threshold “prudential” grounds but should apply meaningful First Amendment scrutiny to whether the investigation is legitimately aimed at deception and whether the compelled disclosures are narrowly justified rather than an instrument of viewpoint-based intimidation.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Viewed in context, New Jersey’s issuance of a consumer-fraud subpoena/CID—backed by ordinary contempt consequences—does not, without more, plausibly convey a Bantam Books-type threat aimed at punishing or suppressing First Choice’s viewpoint rather than gathering evidence in a lawful investigation; the relevant question is whether the State’s words and deeds, taken together, reasonably communicated an intent to retaliate for protected advocacy, and the present posture reflects standard investigative process rather than informal censorship. To the extent the demands compel disclosure that could burden speech or association, the burden must be assessed in degree and in relation to the Attorney General’s asserted enforcement objective (investigating deception) and any confidentiality safeguards, and that calibrated inquiry is ordinarily conducted through the established subpoena-enforcement/quash mechanisms that can narrow, protect, or set aside overbroad requests. A pre-enforcement facial attack on the mere existence of an investigation risks converting routine enforcement tools into a per se First Amendment violation, rather than focusing on whether the particular demands are unduly burdensome, disproportionate, or targeted to suppress protected expression. On these facts, the better course is to require a concrete showing—through the content, manner, and aftermath of the State’s actions—that the investigation is functioning as coercive suppression or that the compelled disclosures impose a substantial associational burden not justified by the State’s enforcement interests.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: New Jersey’s investigative demands are not best understood as regulating non-expressive conduct with only incidental speech effects; when deployed against an advocacy organization’s public-facing messaging and internal advocacy operations, compelled production operates in practice as a direct burden on protected speech and association, with a predictable chilling effect. To the extent the State seeks donor/member-identifying or similarly sensitive internal information, the First Amendment requires exacting scrutiny: the Attorney General must show a sufficiently important interest and a substantial relation, with narrow tailoring rather than a broad “dragnet” demand that can tilt public debate by deterring participation in a disfavored speaker’s advocacy. And because the injury here is the compelled-disclosure burden and resulting chill triggered by the investigation itself—not merely a later prosecution—pre-enforcement review is appropriate; courts should not treat the speech burden as “beside the point” or require the speaker to wait for enforcement when the demand itself is the constitutional harm. On this record, the State has not justified why these compelled disclosures are necessary in scope to a consumer-fraud inquiry, as opposed to more targeted requests that would avoid undue burdens on First Amendment activity.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: New Jersey’s use of consumer-fraud investigative tools to compel a viewpoint-driven nonprofit to disclose internal materials and associational information risks operating as more than an incidental regulatory burden; it functionally coerces and chills protected advocacy by forcing the organization to choose between speaking (and associating) on its own terms or facing coercive process and potential sanctions. Under our compelled-disclosure and associational-privacy cases, the State must at least satisfy exacting scrutiny, including narrow tailoring, and it cannot justify sweeping compelled production merely by invoking a generalized interest in policing “deception” where the demands are broad and the First Amendment injury arises now—through chill and compelled disclosure—before any final enforcement action. A pre-enforcement § 1983/Ex parte Young suit for declaratory and injunctive relief is an ordinary remedial pathway when the investigation itself is the alleged constitutional wrong, and courts should not treat ongoing investigative process as a talisman for deference when it is being used in a way that plausibly penalizes or deters protected expression. Absent a showing that the compelled disclosures are narrowly tailored to a concrete investigative need and not deployed to burden disfavored speech, the First Amendment forbids the State from using its enforcement machinery to exact disclosures that predictably suppress association and advocacy.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The asserted First Amendment injury here arises from New Jersey’s use of ordinary consumer-fraud investigative tools (subpoenas/CIDs) to gather information about allegedly deceptive practices, not from state compulsion forcing the organization to host or associate with another private speaker’s message; that distinction matters because the compelled-hosting/misattribution line of cases (Hurley; Pacific Gas) does not fit this record. The NAACP compelled-membership-disclosure cases likewise do not automatically control because the petitioner has not shown that the State is demanding donor/member lists or comparable associational rosters in a way that predictably triggers reprisals and chill, as opposed to seeking relevant evidence in a conventional fraud inquiry subject to traditional subpoena limits (relevance, legitimate purpose, and undue burden) and state-court quash procedures. Creating a special pre-enforcement First Amendment rule that lets targets bypass ordinary subpoena-enforcement mechanisms whenever they allege “chill” would require courts to engage in unadministrable line-drawing about how intrusive is “too intrusive” at the investigative stage, contrary to clear and workable baseline principles. On these facts and posture, the proper course is to require the petitioner to raise its constitutional objections through the standard motion-to-quash/subpoena-enforcement process absent a concrete showing of viewpoint targeting or compelled disclosure akin to NAACP’s membership-list cases.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The First Amendment, as originally understood and as this Court’s compelled-disclosure cases confirm, does not permit the State to use investigative demands to force an advocacy organization to divulge internal or associational information absent a sufficiently weighty justification and a close fit between the demand and a legitimate law-enforcement objective. On these alleged facts—viewpoint-directed investigation of a pro-life speaker and compelled production that predictably chills speech and association—the CID/subpoena practice operates as a burden on protected expression, triggering heightened scrutiny rather than the deferential standards typical of ordinary civil discovery. A pre-enforcement challenge is justiciable where the State has already invoked compulsory process and the resulting chill and compliance burdens are concrete injuries, and neither “prudential standing” labels nor generalized comity concerns allow federal courts to decline jurisdiction outside Younger’s narrow categories as clarified by Sprint. Because the State’s investigation, as pleaded, is not shown to be narrowly tailored to a non-speech-regulating interest and instead plausibly targets protected advocacy, prospective relief under §1983/Ex parte Young is available.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The asserted First Amendment injury must be matched to the proper doctrinal framework: a consumer-fraud investigation using subpoenas/CIDs is not automatically an “informal censorship” regime under Bantam Books, nor a retaliation claim absent plausible allegations of an adverse action that would not have occurred but for a retaliatory motive. On this record, New Jersey’s use of ordinary investigative tools aimed at probing allegedly deceptive commercial practices looks like standard law-enforcement factfinding, and Petitioner’s generalized chilling-effect allegations do not, by themselves, transform a pre-enforcement challenge into a facial First Amendment bar on investigation. Petitioner remains free to raise tailored First Amendment objections (including associational-privacy and burden arguments) through the subpoena/CID enforcement process, where a court can assess relevance, narrow tailoring, and undue burden without converting “coercion” into a standalone constitutional violation. Because the facts alleged do not yet show the kind of distributor-targeted pressure campaign or procedural suppression mechanisms that Bantam Books condemned, I would reject the broad pre-enforcement First Amendment invalidation Petitioner seeks.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the First Amendment permits a state attorney general to enforce and investigate alleged consumer-fraud “misleading advertising” by a nonprofit advocacy or counseling organization through compelled disclosures/subpoenas, or whether such actions are unconstitutional viewpoint-based burdens on protected speech and associational activity.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. I (free speech and association) and amend. XIV (incorporation); enforcement authority under the New Jersey Consumer Fraud Act (state-law basis for the subpoena/investigation referenced in the record).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: First Choice argues that New Jersey’s consumer-fraud investigation—particularly the subpoena/compelled production and related enforcement steps—targets and chills its constitutionally protected speech (including pro-life counseling/advocacy) and expressive association; that applying a consumer-fraud framework to its communications operates as viewpoint discrimination or, at minimum, triggers heightened First Amendment scrutiny; and that federal courts should provide timely injunctive/constitutional relief rather than deferring to state processes that functionally prolong a speech-burdening restraint.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The Attorney General argues that the investigation and subpoena are routine, content-neutral law-enforcement tools aimed at preventing deception and protecting consumers, not suppressing a viewpoint; that compelled production in an investigation is permissible when relevant to enforcing generally applicable fraud laws; and that federal-court intervention is improper or premature because the matter can be addressed through state-court procedures (including challenges to the subpoena) without extraordinary federal equitable relief.
key_precedents: Lexmark Int’l, Inc. v. Static Control Components, Inc., 572 U.S. 118 (2014)
Platkin v. Smith & Wesson Sales, 474 N.J. Super. 476 (App. Div. 2023)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that Bantam Books demands a context-sensitive inquiry and that fraud prevention is a sufficiently important interest, but those points do not relieve the State of its burden under our compelled-disclosure and associational-privacy cases to show a substantial relation and tailoring commensurate with the deterrent effect. Even accepting her concern about practical pressure on intermediaries, the record still reflects a broad, up-front collection/compulsion regime justified largely by administrative convenience rather than a demonstrated need that narrower, as-needed tools could not meet. As Justice Kavanaugh stresses, we can resolve the case on the absence of narrow tailoring without casting doubt on legitimate anti-fraud enforcement generally, and that approach best fits our exacting-scrutiny framework. Justice Jackson’s worry about insufficient quantification of chill is fair, but our precedents do not require plaintiffs to wait for concrete reprisals where the scheme predictably deters association and the State offers no meaningful limiting principle.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Bantam Books framework usefully highlights that context can reveal coercion, but it does not resolve the antecedent First Amendment defect here: compelled disclosure that predictably chills association and anonymity is itself a burden on protected activity and triggers the most searching justification. Even accepting the State’s anti-fraud interest, Chief Justice Roberts is right that the State must show a substantial relation and narrow tailoring; broad, up-front collection justified by enforcement convenience falls short where less intrusive, as-needed mechanisms are available. Justice Kagan’s editorial-discretion point underscores that the regime also risks commandeering expressive choices, which only reinforces the need for narrow tailoring rather than diluting scrutiny. On this record, the State has not carried its burden under our associational-privacy precedents, and I see no principled doctrinal basis to treat this compelled disclosure as a lesser First Amendment interest.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Bantam Books point is the strongest for Respondent, but it still requires a record showing that the State’s communications—considered in context—carried an implicit threat of concrete adverse action sufficient to coerce intermediaries, and I do not see that predicate established here. Even assuming an important anti-fraud interest, I agree with Chief Justice Roberts that broad, up-front collection or compulsion justified largely by administrative convenience fails exacting scrutiny because the State has not shown why narrower, as-needed tools would be inadequate. Justice Kagan’s editorial-discretion framing underscores the First Amendment interests at stake, but it does not supply the missing demonstration that this sweeping regime is necessary rather than simply easier to administer. A narrow ruling for Petitioner on lack of tailoring, as Justice Kavanaugh suggests, respects NAACP v. Alabama–type associational protections without casting doubt on ordinary, properly tailored enforcement.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s narrow-tailoring critique is the most serious point against Respondent, but it presupposes that we are in a conventional compelled-disclosure case and not a Bantam Books coercion/suppression case where the threshold question is whether officials, in context, leveraged governmental power to induce intermediaries to suppress protected advocacy. Even if the State invokes fraud prevention or “business practices,” that label does not remove First Amendment scrutiny when the practical aim or predictable effect is self-censorship, and our inquiry remains contextual—“who said what and how, and what reaction followed”—not a rigid checklist. Justice Barrett and Justice Alito emphasize gaps in the record on coercive indicia, but on this posture Petitioners have not offered a principled doctrinal distinction that would take the challenged conduct outside Bantam Books’ framework or justify treating suppression pressure as mere administrative convenience. Accordingly, I would adhere to Respondent, while recognizing that tailoring analysis may become decisive if the case is reframed or further developed on remand.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The strongest point on the other side—pressed by Chief Justice Roberts and echoed by Justice Kavanaugh—is that even under exacting scrutiny the State has not shown narrow tailoring and cannot rely on administrative convenience for broad, up-front collection. But that argument, as Justice Sotomayor emphasizes, assumes this is merely a compelled-disclosure regime aimed at nonexpressive conduct; here the practical operation is to supervise and predictably pressure editorial/curatorial judgments about what speech to present and how, which our Hurley line treats as expressive activity. Once the State is effectively attempting to reshape the “mix of messages,” anti-fraud interests cannot be pursued through a scheme that chills and deters protected moderation choices, and Zauderer-style reasoning does not license an “unduly burdensome” apparatus of compelled explanations in that domain. Absent a limiting principle that keeps the State from leveraging this tool to influence content decisions, I would not join a narrow-tailoring reversal that misses the First Amendment character of the burden.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that Bantam Books demands a contextual inquiry into whether government has leveraged its power to induce private censorship, and labels like “fraud prevention” cannot launder coercion. But even accepting that framework, the State’s regime here still operates through compelled disclosure/collection that predictably chills association, and under NAACP v. Alabama and our exacting-scrutiny cases the State must show a substantial relation and narrow tailoring—not merely administrative convenience. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh stress, the record lacks a concrete demonstration that less speech-burdening, as-needed tools would fail, which is the relevant constitutional deficiency whether we characterize the burden as compulsion or coercive pressure. Nothing Justice Kagan adds about editorial discretion supplies a doctrinal basis to uphold sweeping, up-front compulsion where the State has not justified why narrower alternatives cannot serve its interest.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Bantam Books point rightly emphasizes context and the risk that government pressure on intermediaries can chill speech without formal compulsion. But even taking that framework seriously, this case still fits comfortably within our compelled-disclosure/associational-privacy line: under exacting scrutiny the State must show a substantial relation and tailoring, and—consistent with Chief Justice Roberts’s point—administrative convenience and up-front mass collection are not a substitute for demonstrating why narrower, as-needed tools would fail. The respondent-side reframing (Justice Kagan’s editorial-discretion emphasis) does not supply a workable doctrinal basis to uphold a broad regime on this record without diluting NAACP v. Alabama–type protections. The institutionally restrained path is a narrow holding for Petitioner on lack of tailoring, leaving room for targeted anti-fraud enforcement mechanisms.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s Bantam Books point is the strongest for Respondent: context can convert “requests” into coercion when backed by implicit threats. But as Justice Alito and the Chief Justice both stress, that framework is record-dependent, and I do not see sufficiently developed indicia here—clear assertions of enforcement authority tied to noncompliance, concrete adverse consequences, or a pattern showing officials were effectively commandeering intermediaries rather than regulating through ordinary channels. Even accepting fraud prevention as an important interest, Chief Justice Roberts is right that exacting scrutiny still requires a substantial relation and tailoring; broad, up-front collection or compulsion justified mainly by administrative convenience cannot be sustained when narrower, as-needed tools are not shown inadequate. Absent a principled, precedent-based distinction from the NAACP v. Alabama associational-privacy line on this record, I remain with Petitioner on a narrow, tailoring-focused disposition.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s narrow-tailoring critique is the strongest case for Petitioner, but it still seems to rest on assumptions about administrable “as-needed” alternatives and a deterrent/chilling effect that the present record does not concretely establish; I am wary of converting an asserted preference for enforcement design into a constitutional mandate without that grounding. Justice Sotomayor’s contextual focus on how state power operates in practice remains salient to me: whether regulated entities reasonably perceive the regime as coercive or suppressive is a procedural-fairness inquiry that our First Amendment doctrine cannot ignore. Even accepting that exacting scrutiny applies, I do not yet see the kind of record-based showing that the State’s prophylactic approach is overbroad in operation rather than simply broad in design. On this conference showing, I would adhere to Respondent and address tailoring in a way that keeps open as-applied challenges where concrete chilling or coercion is demonstrated.
